title: C language reference: keywords, tokens and translation phases
learningObjectives: Explain the topic and its C rules.
Trace the example and identify its purpose.
Identify important validation and failure cases.
Apply the concept in a tested program or reference exercise.

understand.concept: C source is translated through phases that include character mapping, preprocessing, tokenization, syntax and semantic analysis, translation to implementation output and linking. Keywords are reserved tokens with defined grammatical roles; identifiers and literals follow lexical rules.
understand.whyItMatters: Understanding tokens and translation phases helps diagnose why source text is interpreted differently than expected and clarifies the roles of preprocessing, compilation and linking.
understand.analogy: Treat the project or language feature as a set of components with explicit interfaces and responsibilities.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal language, library and resource-management rules.

explain.narrative:
C source is translated through phases that include character mapping, preprocessing, tokenization, syntax and semantic analysis, translation to implementation output and linking. Keywords are reserved tokens with defined grammatical roles; identifiers and literals follow lexical rules.

For a complete implementation, define input constraints, ownership, error handling and test cases before coding. Compile with warnings and verify normal, boundary and failure behaviour.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The preprocessor handles the include and macro directive before later translation stages. The compiler then parses tokens such as for, int, identifiers, constants and string literals.

practise.guidedTask: Classify keywords, identifiers, punctuators and literals in the example.
practise.independentTask: Explain how a macro is expanded before the compiler parses the resulting translation unit.
hints: Keywords cannot be used as ordinary identifiers in the same grammatical context.
Preprocessing is not the same as linking.
Use compiler preprocessing output when diagnosing macro expansion.
